title: Sheet mulching a new bed
subtitle: Cardboard, compost, and time convert lawn to planting ground.
excerpt: Sheet mulching (also called lasagne gardening) layers cardboard and organic matter over existing ground to kill turf and weeds without digging. A well-built sheet-mulched bed is ready to plant in one to two seasons.
sourceNotes: Method after Charles Dowding's writings on mulching and conversion beds (2007-2024). Cardboard-as-weed-suppressant approach widely documented in UK organic growing guides from the 1990s onwards. Slug behaviour in damp mulch from RHS pest management guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: A method of converting grass or weedy ground to a growing bed by covering it with overlapping cardboard and organic matter, excluding light and smothering the existing vegetation.
A colloquial name for sheet mulching, referring to the layered structure of cardboard, compost, straw, and other organic materials built up like pasta sheets.

content.text: converts lawn or rough ground into a planting bed by covering it with overlapping cardboard and a thick layer of organic matter. The cardboard excludes light and kills the turf below. The organic matter gives you something to plant into. No digging, no herbicide, no rotovating.
Autumn is the best time to lay a
bed. The turf breaks down over winter and the bed is workable by spring. A spring-built bed needs a deeper compost layer (at least 15 cm) to plant into immediately.

The method works on lawn, rough grass, overgrown plots, and even gravel paths. The main constraint is the weed population underneath. Annual weeds and grass die reliably within one season. Persistent perennial weeds (bindweed, Japanese knotweed, horsetail) require 12 to 24 months of light exclusion, and horsetail may need longer.

items.name: Cardboard (plain brown, unprinted)
items.qty: enough to cover the area with 20 cm overlaps at every joint
items.substitutions: several layers of thick newspaper work, but cardboard lasts longer

items.name: Compost (well-rotted)
items.qty: 10-15 cm layer on top of cardboard

items.name: Woodchip or straw
items.qty: optional 5-8 cm layer between compost and cardboard to add bulk

items.name: Manure (well-rotted)
items.qty: optional additional layer under the compost

content.text: Mow or cut down any tall growth first. It does not need to be removed. Lay the cardboard directly on top, overlapping each sheet by at least 20 cm. Look for gaps carefully: a 5 cm gap lets in enough light for bindweed or couch grass to push through.
Water the cardboard thoroughly before adding the next layer. Dry cardboard is stiff and tends to lift at the edges. Wet cardboard lies flat, bonds with the ground, and decomposes faster.
Apply compost directly on top. A 10 cm layer is the minimum to plant transplants. For direct sowing, add 5 cm more. Spread the compost evenly, filling in around any gaps. Do not compress it heavily.

attrs.title: Sourcing cardboard for large areas
attrs.body: Supermarkets, electrical retailers, and online delivery depots produce large quantities of plain cardboard. Ask the back-of-store staff before the delivery boxes go to the recycling compactor. Avoid boxes with glossy printing, laminated coatings, or staple strips. Tape is fine; remove it before laying.

content.text: For autumn-built beds, wait until spring. By March or April the cardboard is soft, the turf below is dead or dying, and worms have begun to move up into the compost layer. Plant transplants by pushing through the compost into the softened cardboard below.

For a bed built in spring with 15 cm of compost, courgettes, squash, beans, and brassica transplants all establish well. Avoid root vegetables in the first season; the cardboard barrier blocks downward root growth for parsnips and carrots.

attrs.heading: When it goes wrong
attrs.intro: Most failures are coverage or timing issues.

items.symptom: Weeds pushing up through the compost
items.cause: Cardboard gaps, or weed seeds present in the compost itself.
items.fix: Patch cardboard gaps with offcuts weighted with extra compost. Hoe off compost-layer weeds while they are small seedlings. These are surface weeds from the compost, not the suppressed layer below.

items.symptom: Cardboard blew away before I added compost
items.cause: Dry cardboard on a windy day.
items.fix: Re-wet it and add compost the same day. Keep a watering can ready when laying on open ground in dry weather.

items.cause: A thick damp organic surface is good slug habitat.
items.fix: Allow the surface to dry between rains before planting. Plant out slightly larger transplants so they are past the most vulnerable stage. Use grit or copper tape around beds where slugs are a persistent problem.

items.cause: One season is rarely enough to exhaust deep bindweed roots.
items.fix: Continue light exclusion. Top up the compost layer. Pull any shoots that break through before they unfurl leaves. Do not let them photosynthesise; roots will starve eventually without light.
